overview.title: Training the custom TensorFlow model, and the PyTorch train_step()
overview.section: 7.4 Writing your own training and evaluation loops
overview.subsection: 7.4.4 Using fit() with a custom training loop
overview.main_topic: A reusable get_custom_model() factory that builds a Functional MNIST classifier inside CustomModel and compiles it with only an optimizer; training it with fit(); and the PyTorch version of the overridden train_step().
overview.central_idea: The same Keras contract (train_step returns a logs dict, metrics property lists trackers) holds across backends; only the gradient mechanism changes. In PyTorch it is loss.backward(), reading each variable's .value.grad, and applying updates under torch.no_grad().
overview.importance: It demonstrates concretely that a Functional model can be wrapped in a custom-trained Model subclass, and it shows the backend-specific part of a custom step for PyTorch in its entirety.
learning_objectives: Read get_custom_model(): a 784-512-10 Functional network with dropout, wrapped in CustomModel(inputs, outputs).
Explain why compile() receives only keras.optimizers.Adam().
Write a PyTorch train_step(): forward pass, loss.backward(), collect gradients from v.value.grad, optimizer.apply under torch.no_grad().
Compare the PyTorch and TensorFlow versions line by line.
Recognize that calling fit() is identical whichever backend's train_step is used.
prerequisites: The PyTorch training step function from 7.4.2 (p.241-242).
Dense, Dropout and softmax for MNIST classification.

summary:
The page continues *Customizing fit() with TensorFlow* by packaging the model definition into a **reusable function, `get_custom_model()`**. It builds a Functional graph: `keras.Input(shape=(28 * 28,))`, a `Dense(512, activation="relu")` layer, `Dropout(0.5)`, and a `Dense(10, activation="softmax")` output. Instead of `keras.Model(inputs, outputs)` it calls **`CustomModel(inputs, outputs)`**, so the Functional network gets the custom `train_step()` from Listing 7.21. It compiles with `optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam()` only, because the loss is defined outside the model, and returns the model. Training is then a plain `model.fit(train_images, train_labels, epochs=3)`.

Under *Customizing fit() with PyTorch*, the authors give the PyTorch `CustomModel`. The module-level `loss_fn` and `loss_tracker` are the same. In `train_step()` the forward pass (`self(inputs, training=True)`) and the loss are computed normally (callout: *runs the forward pass*). Then `loss.backward()` populates gradients, and the gradients are **retrieved** by listing the trainable weights and reading `v.value.grad` for each, since a Keras variable wraps a torch tensor in its `.value`. The weights are **updated** with `self.optimizer.apply(gradients, trainable_weights)` inside `with torch.no_grad():`, so the update itself is not tracked by autograd. The loss tracker is updated and `{"loss": loss_tracker.result()}` is returned; the `metrics` property again lists `loss_tracker`.

The page ends with the identical two lines `model = get_custom_model()` and `model.fit(train_images, train_labels, epochs=3)`. When this runs with the PyTorch backend, `get_custom_model()` picks up the PyTorch `CustomModel` that was just defined. The JAX version follows on p.249.

concepts.name: Overriding train_step()
concepts.definition: Redefining Model.train_step(), called by fit() per batch, to implement a custom algorithm.
concepts.intuition: Swap the loop body, keep the loop.
concepts.technical: Here implemented with PyTorch autograd: forward, loss.backward(), gather v.value.grad, optimizer.apply under torch.no_grad(), update metrics, return logs.
concepts.significance: Same pattern across TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX.
concepts.example: The PyTorch CustomModel on this page.
concepts.misconception: That the PyTorch version needs to call optimizer.zero_grad(); the page's code does not, as Keras's optimizer handles gradients it is given. (The book does not discuss gradient zeroing here.)

concepts.name: Functional API inside a custom Model subclass
concepts.definition: Building a graph of layers from keras.Input to outputs and passing it to a Model subclass's constructor.
concepts.intuition: The architecture is a blueprint; the subclass decides how it is trained.
concepts.technical: CustomModel(inputs, outputs) invokes the inherited Functional constructor of keras.Model.
concepts.significance: You keep Functional conveniences while customizing training.
concepts.misconception: That subclassing Model forces you to write call() yourself.

concepts.name: Dropout
concepts.definition: A layer that randomly zeroes a fraction of its inputs during training.
concepts.intuition: Prevents the network from relying on any single feature.
concepts.technical: Dropout(0.5) drops half of the 512 features at training time and is inactive at inference; train_step's training=True turns it on.
concepts.significance: Explains why the training flag must be passed in train_step.
concepts.misconception: That dropout is active during evaluate() or predict(); it is not.

concepts.name: PyTorch-style backward pass
concepts.definition: loss.backward() computes gradients of the loss and stores them on the tensors that require grad.
concepts.intuition: The forward pass leaves breadcrumbs; backward follows them in reverse.
concepts.technical: Gradients are accessed via v.value.grad on Keras variables, then passed to self.optimizer.apply.
concepts.significance: The backend-specific core of the PyTorch train_step.
concepts.misconception: That backward() returns the gradients; it returns None and stores them as attributes.

code.title: Reusable model factory get_custom_model()
code.original_code:
def get_custom_model():
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=(28 * 28,))
    features = layers.Dense(512, activation="relu")(inputs)
    features = layers.Dropout(0.5)(features)
    outputs = layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")(features)
    model = CustomModel(inputs, outputs)
    model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam())
    return model
code.what_it_does: Builds a Functional MNIST classifier, wraps it in CustomModel so it uses the overridden train_step, compiles it with Adam only, and returns it.

line_explanations.explanation: Hidden Dense layer of 512 relu units followed by Dropout(0.5).
10-way softmax output producing class probabilities, matching SparseCategoricalCrossentropy's default from_logits=False.
CustomModel instead of keras.Model: same Functional constructor, custom train_step.
Only an optimizer is passed, since loss_fn and loss_tracker are used directly inside train_step (p.247).

code.inputs_outputs: No inputs; returns a compiled CustomModel.
code.theory_link: Demonstrates the p.247 note that custom train_step works with Functional models.

pitfalls: CustomModel is resolved at call time, so the version defined most recently is used; re-run the right definition before calling get_custom_model().

code.title: Customizing fit(): PyTorch version
code.original_code:
import keras
from keras import layers

loss_fn = keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy()
loss_tracker = keras.metrics.Mean(name="loss")

class CustomModel(keras.Model):
    def train_step(self, data):
        inputs, targets = data
        predictions = self(inputs, training=True)
        loss = loss_fn(targets, predictions)

        loss.backward()
        trainable_weights = [v for v in self.trainable_weights]
        gradients = [v.value.grad for v in trainable_weights]

        with torch.no_grad():
            self.optimizer.apply(gradients, trainable_weights)

        loss_tracker.update_state(loss)
        return {"loss": loss_tracker.result()}

    @property
    def metrics(self):
        return [loss_tracker]
code.what_it_does: Defines the PyTorch-backend CustomModel whose train_step uses PyTorch autograd for gradients while staying inside fit().

line_explanations.explanation: Same module-level loss function and loss tracker as the TensorFlow version.
Callout: runs the forward pass. No tape is needed; PyTorch records the graph automatically.
Callout: retrieves the gradients. backward() fills .grad on each underlying torch tensor; v.value is the torch tensor inside a Keras variable.
Callout: updates weights. torch.no_grad() prevents autograd from tracking the in-place weight update.
Callout: returns the average loss so far by querying the loss tracker metric.
metrics property, so fit() resets loss_tracker each epoch and at the start of evaluate().

code.inputs_outputs: Input: batch (inputs, targets). Output: {"loss": running mean}. Side effect: weights updated.
code.algorithm: Forward -> loss -> backward -> collect grads -> optimizer.apply (no_grad) -> metric update -> logs.
code.theory_link: Same three-step loop as p.239; PyTorch's imperative autograd replaces the TensorFlow tape.

deeper.title: TensorFlow vs PyTorch train_step, line by line
deeper.body:
| Step | TensorFlow (p.247) | PyTorch (p.248) |
|---|---|---|
| Forward | inside `with tf.GradientTape() as tape:` | plain call |
| Gradients | `tape.gradient(loss, self.trainable_weights)` | `loss.backward()` then `[v.value.grad for v in ...]` |
| Update | `self.optimizer.apply(...)` | same, inside `torch.no_grad()` |
| Metrics / return | identical | identical |

The comparison is an editorial summary of the two listings.

deeper.title: Why the update runs under torch.no_grad()
deeper.body: Beyond the book: weights in PyTorch are tensors with `requires_grad=True`. Modifying them in place while autograd is recording would (a) be recorded as part of a graph and (b) typically raise an error for in-place operations on leaf tensors that require grad. `torch.no_grad()` tells PyTorch that this arithmetic is bookkeeping, not part of the model's differentiable computation.

Training is the usual model.fit(train_images, train_labels, epochs=3).
PyTorch's train_step: forward, loss.backward(), gradients from v.value.grad, optimizer.apply inside torch.no_grad().
Metric handling (loss_tracker, metrics property, returned dict) is identical across backends.

questions.question: In the PyTorch train_step, how are the gradients obtained?
options: By calling loss.backward() and then reading v.value.grad for each trainable weight
questions.answer: By calling loss.backward() and then reading v.value.grad for each trainable weight
questions.explanation: That is the code on the page. tape.gradient is TensorFlow's way; jax.grad is JAX's; compute_gradients is not used here.

questions.question: Why is self.optimizer.apply() wrapped in torch.no_grad()?
questions.answer: So that the weight update is not tracked by PyTorch's autograd; it is a bookkeeping operation, not part of the differentiable computation.
questions.explanation: The callout says 'Updates weights'; the no_grad context ensures autograd ignores this step.

questions.question: Why does get_custom_model() call CustomModel(inputs, outputs) instead of keras.Model(inputs, outputs)?
questions.answer: So the Functional network uses the overridden train_step() of CustomModel when fit() is called.
questions.explanation: CustomModel inherits the Functional constructor and adds only the custom training step.

questions.question: How many trainable parameters does the model built by get_custom_model() have?
questions.explanation: Dense layers have weights plus biases; Dropout has no parameters.

questions.question: Which line is identical in the TensorFlow and PyTorch train_step implementations?
questions.explanation: The metric update and returned dict are shared; the other three are backend-specific.

questions.question: Why is training=True passed in self(inputs, training=True) for this model in particular?
questions.answer: Because the model contains Dropout(0.5), which must be active during training and inactive at inference.
questions.explanation: The training flag selects the training behavior of such layers.

questions.question: Could you explain to someone why the exact same two lines train both the TensorFlow and PyTorch custom models?
questions.answer: fit() only calls train_step and reads the returned dict; get_custom_model() picks up whichever CustomModel is currently defined.
questions.explanation: This is the separation of concerns the train_step pattern provides.
